statement: In 12 men with severe cocaine dependence (10 of them injecting daily) who stopped using in a closed residential research unit in Baltimore, compared with 10 men with no history of drug abuse or dependence living on the same unit (Weddington et al., 1990), the first 28 days without cocaine are associated with mood distress, depression scores and craving that were highest on admission day, within 48 hours of the last use, and lower over the following four weeks, mostly within about two weeks; the authors describe the fall as steady and saw no phases. Self-rated sleep did not differ from the comparison group except more difficulty falling asleep throughout and a larger improvement over time in feeling clear-headed on waking, and both groups slept better over time, which the authors partly put down to getting used to the unit; resting heart rate was lower at first and rose by about 11 beats a minute, and weight gain did not differ. This disagrees with an earlier clinical description, from 30 outpatients' interviews and recollections, of a crash followed by 1 to 10 weeks in which, after a few near-normal days, low pleasure, low energy, anxiety and craving return (Gawin & Kleber, 1986). The settings differ: the residential unit had no cocaine and none of the people, places or objects that set off craving, and the plotted means of several mood scales in the residential study rise again around days 7 to 9 before falling, a pattern its text does not discuss and no test examined. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: Twelve men who stopped cocaine while living in a locked research unit felt worst, and wanted cocaine most, on the day they arrived; over the next four weeks this slowly got better, mostly in the first two weeks. Their sleep was much like that of the 10 men without drug problems living there, except that falling asleep was harder. An older study of people stopping at home described craving coming back after a few calm days. The unit had no cocaine and nothing to remind the men of it, which may explain the difference.
population: Men with severe cocaine dependence (mostly daily injecting) in a closed residential research unit in Baltimore, 1987-88, and men without drug dependence on the same unit
exposure: The first 28 days without cocaine, starting within 48 hours of last use
comparator: Ten men without substance dependence (except nicotine) living on the same unit; for the course over time, the cocaine group's own earlier ratings
outcome: Self-rated mood (Profile of Mood States, Beck Depression Inventory), craving (cocaine group only), sleep (St Mary's Sleep Questionnaire), heart rate, blood pressure and weight on 11 days
magnitude: F ratios only (mixed ANOVA): Beck depression group 13.949, time 10.670, interaction 8.526; total mood distress 5.082, 9.359, 5.537; craving over time 17.270 (all P<.05 or smaller); difficulty falling asleep, group 10.428; heart rate +10.9 against −2.3 beats a minute; weight gain 4.6 against 3.8 kg, not different.

evidence.locator: Subjects and Methods › Subjects, 8th and 9th paragraphs (p. 862); Research Procedures, 3rd paragraph (p. 863); Table 1 (p. 863)
evidence.extracted: Of thirty men with cocaine dependence who made appointments, sixteen came, fourteen were admitted and 12 completed; ten controls completed; measures were taken on days 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 14, 18, 21, 25 and 28 between 9 AM and noon; 10 of the 12 injected cocaine; antisocial personality disorder 58% against none in controls.

evidence.locator: Outcome › Mood Scores; Craving for Cocaine (p. 864); Table 2 and Figure 2 (p. 865)
evidence.extracted: Mood distress and Beck depression scores were higher in the cocaine group and fell over time more than in controls (Beck depression F = 13.949 for group, 10.670 for time, 8.526 for interaction; total mood distress 5.082, 9.359, 5.537); craving was highest on admission day and fell significantly over the 28 days (F = 17.270, df 10,110).

evidence.locator: Outcome › Self-reports of Sleep; Weight, Heart Rate, and Blood Pressure (p. 864, continued p. 866); Table 2 (p. 865)
evidence.extracted: Sleep reports did not differ from controls except more difficulty falling asleep in the cocaine group throughout (group F = 10.428) and a greater improvement in clear-headedness on arising in the cocaine group (interaction F = 2.001); the other sleep measures improved over time in both groups; weight gain of 4.6 kg against 3.8 kg did not differ; heart rate rose 10.9 beats a minute in the cocaine group and fell 2.3 in controls.

The authors report that mood, craving and night waking improved gradually and were not cyclical or phasic in the first 4 weeks, unlike the earlier phase models, and suggest that the controlled setting, without cocaine or drug-taking cues, may explain the difference.

In the plotted means, several Profile of Mood States scales in the cocaine group fall from day 1 to day 5, rise again around days 7 to 9 and then fall and stay low from about the second week; the paper reports no test of a phasic pattern (editors' reading of the figure; no values extracted).

Limitations named by the authors: a small all-male, mostly Black sample of mostly daily injectors; self-report; the experimental environment, which kept out the people and situations that could trigger conditioned responses; no standard last dose; only the first month; morning measures only.

evidence.locator: Figure and legend (p. 110); Phase 2: Withdrawal, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 111)
evidence.extracted: In outpatients, the crash was followed by one to five days of near-normal mood and sleep with little craving, then a fluctuating period of anhedonia, low energy, anxiety and irritability in which craving returned, lasting one to ten or more weeks (1 to 10 weeks in the figure); earlier attempts to stop had all failed within several days of this phase beginning.

risk_of_bias.note: Completers only, in a locked unit; unblinded self-ratings every 2 to 4 days; confounding by personality disorder and staff attention; the earlier description relies on non-blind clinicians and recollection.

inconsistency.note: The residential study's steady course disagrees with the outpatient description of returning craving; the explanation offered (setting) is untested.

indirectness.note: Worded for the residential setting and named outpatient setting studied.

imprecision.note: Twelve men and ten controls; F ratios without effect sizes or intervals.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low. Risk of bias −1, inconsistency −1 and imprecision −1 give very low. Status mixed: two studies disagree, the residential study's explanation (a setting without cocaine or cues) has not been tested, and its own figure shows a second rise on some mood scales that no analysis examined.
